surface: text-CHECK pseudo-enums vs real Postgres enums (exhaustiveness coverage)
claim: The schema uses two different mechanisms for closed value sets and only one of them can be checked at compile time. FIVE real Postgres enums (app_role, application_status, auto_tip_mode, job_category, job_status) generate into types.ts as string unions PLUS a runtime Constants array, which is what lets src/test/jobStatusExhaustive.test.ts enumerate job_status from its source of truth and assert every label/colour map covers every member. TWENTY-TWO other closed sets are text columns with CHECK (x = ANY (ARRAY[...])) instead, so they generate as bare 'string' -- no union, no Constants entry, no assertNever possible, and no equivalent guard test. The two most consequential are jobs.payment_status (10 values: unpaid, escrow, payout_pending, released, refunded, cancelled, abandoned, failed, chargeback, cancelling -- the escrow state machine) and notifications.type (17 values). The jobStatusExhaustive test exists precisely because pending_approval once fell through every branch and rendered an empty box, twice; the same failure mode is currently unguardable for payment_status.

surface: public.user_roles RLS: 'Deny all deletes to user_roles' is a PERMISSIVE no-op
claim: user_roles carries a policy named 'Deny all deletes to user_roles' with USING (false), but it is declared PERMISSIVE, not RESTRICTIVE. Permissive policies are OR-ed together, so a permissive USING(false) contributes nothing at all: it can never subtract access. DELETE on user_roles is therefore governed entirely by the sibling 'Admins can delete roles' policy, exactly as if the deny policy did not exist. The current net behaviour is probably the intended one (admins may delete roles), so this is not an open hole -- it is a security control that reads as a hard stop, is named as a hard stop, and enforces nothing. That is the 'configured but does nothing' class, and on the table that grants admin. Note the contrast with its twin: 'Deny all updates to user_roles' is also permissive-false, but it happens to be the ONLY permissive UPDATE policy on the table, so updates really are denied -- by the absence of any passing policy, not by the deny. Two policies written the same way, one working by accident and one inert. Routed to lh-authz-rls as the owning lane.
repro: SELECT polname, polcmd, polpermissive, pg_get_expr(polqual, polrelid) FROM pg_policy WHERE polrelid='public.user_roles'::regclass on prod fncmgoasalhdgfwzhsqa returns 6 rows. polcmd='d': 'Admins can delete roles' PERMISSIVE USING has_role((SELECT auth.uid()),'admin'), and 'Deny all deletes to user_roles' PERMISSIVE USING false. polcmd='w': only 'Deny all updates to user_roles' PERMISSIVE USING false WITH CHECK false. No RESTRICTIVE policy exists on the table.

The two element-not-found specs seed date_needed as a full ISO timestamp (new Date(...).toISOString()) into a mocked jobs row, but prod jobs.date_needed is a Postgres 'date' NOT NULL (verified: information_schema.columns on fncmgoasalhdgfwzhsqa), so PostgREST only ever returns bare YYYY-MM-DD. claim: Both sites drop the Supabase error and then check ONLY the zero-row case — which means the case they were written to catch is the one they miss. Both do: const { data: rows } = await supabase.from('jobs').update(...).select('id'); if (rows && rows.length === 0) report(...). When the write genuinely FAILS (RLS denial, network, PGRST202) supabase-js returns { data: null, error: <err> }, so rows is null, the guard 'rows && rows.length === 0' is FALSE, and nothing is reported at all. The comment at useJobMediaUpload.ts:220 says 'ignore any error, but still surface a silent zero-row rejection so it's visible in logs' — the intent is right, the implementation reports the benign half and swallows the real half. surface: post-job checkout window → captured amount vs jobs.budget
claim: jobs.budget stays poster-writable while payment_status='unpaid' (enforce_poster_jobs_money_lock only locks once funded — verified live via pg_get_functiondef on prod), and the Stripe Checkout line items are frozen at session creation. A poster who edits budget between create-payment's session creation and paying is charged the OLD amount while every downstream payout computes from the NEW jobs.budget. Inflation is caught only because payouts link source_transaction (transfer > charge is rejected by Stripe) — but that link is best-effort inside a try/catch (process-scheduled-payouts:539-550 'Could not link charge' warn-and-continue), so a transient Stripe read failure turns the cap off and the inflated transfer draws from the platform balance. Deflation (lower budget after session creation) silently over-charges the poster with no reconciliation. Nothing at funding time compares pi.amount_received against budget+fees.
repro: Live: pg_get_functiondef(enforce_poster_jobs_money_lock) on prod shows the funded-only gate; code: create-payment/index.ts:420-435 freezes line items, checkoutSessionCompleted.ts:651-744 records funding without amount reconciliation, process-scheduled-payouts/index.ts:539-550 best-effort source_transaction.

note: REFINED after reading release-payout: that path already hard-caps payout at pi.amount_received (release-payout/index.ts:561-596) and documents this exact budget-edit hazard. Residual gap: (a) process-scheduled-payouts has NO explicit captured-amount cap — only best-effort source_transaction inside try/catch — so the two payout paths disagree on a guard both need; (b) the funding webhook never reconciles captured vs budget, so poster-deflation over-charge remains invisible. Fix: add the same cap to process-scheduled-payouts.

surface: charge-recurring-visits → Stripe Tax transactions never registered + fee floor excludes tax
claim: (a) Tax on recurring visits is computed via stripe.tax.calculations.create and charged inside totalCents, but tax.transactions.createFromCalculation is never called anywhere in the repo (0 grep hits) — LA sales tax collected on recurring assembly/handyman visits never reaches Stripe Tax's filing reports, and calculations expire (~90d) so they cannot be committed retroactively. Fix is ordering: compute tax first, pass as otherChargeCents.

claim: A pg_cron job that fails INTERMITTENTLY alerts nobody. sweep_dead_crons() only emits an 'erroring' verdict when the last 3 recorded runs ALL have status <> 'succeeded'; a job that fails once a day out of 24 hourly runs never trips it, and pg_cron's own failure record is written to cron.job_run_details, which nothing else reads. Proven live by the very failure this lane found: sweep-silent-cron-failures raised on 2026-09-01 08:47 and the app produced no signal at all — no error_logs row, no Slack alert, nothing. It also means a SQL cron that raises every day at the same hour is indistinguishable from a healthy one on every dashboard the app has.
repro: PROD fncmgoasalhdgfwzhsqa. 1) select count(*) from cron.job_run_details d join cron.job j on j.jobid=d.jobid where j.jobname='sweep-silent-cron-failures' and d.status='failed' => 1 (2026-09-01 08:47). 2) select count(*) from error_logs where tags->>'source' in ('cron-dead','cron-silent') => 0 rows, ever — no row was written for that failure or for anything else. 3) The gate is in the function body: sweep_dead_crons() computes recent_bad over LIMIT 3 and requires recent_total >= 3 AND recent_bad = recent_total before it will say 'erroring'.
evidence: cron.job_run_details failed-run row; zero error_logs rows with source cron-dead/cron-silent since the detectors were created 2026-08-26; pg_get_functiondef(sweep_dead_crons) recent_bad/recent_total predicate

claim: extend-boosts-hourly is the only one of the 42 scheduled pg_cron jobs with no row in cron_work_expectations, so sweep_dead_crons() — which iterates the expectations table, not cron.job — cannot see it.
